clue.text: G&S production line, on which 10's written articles

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece sitting on another is placed above it, so the figure comes first

parts.note: the number 10 written out looks like the letters I and O
an is the indefinite article
the is the definite article, the second of the two articles

explanation.surface: A note about a Gilbert and Sullivan show, with the puzzle's honoree having written pieces about it.
explanation.walkthrough: '10' looks like a cross-reference to the theme answer, but here it is just the figures 1 and 0 read as the letters I and O.
explanation.definitionFit: Iolanthe is one of the comic operas Gilbert and Sullivan wrote together, so it is an example of a G&S production.

clue.text: Perhaps Maudling and Hill forgetting to say Linda's worried

indicators.note: forgetting means the following word is dropped from the hill

parts.note: a tor is a rocky hill, as on Dartmoor
say means for example, abbreviated e.g.

indicators.note: worried means agitated, so these letters are shaken into a new order

explanation.surface: Two politicians or writers, one of whom forgets to mention that Linda is anxious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maudling and Hill' looks like a pair of Reginalds as the definition, but 'Hill' is wordplay. Reginald Maudling was a Conservative Chancellor; in the sitcom Linda is Reggie Perrin's daughter.
explanation.definitionFit: The Conservative politician Maudling's first name makes him one example of a man so named.

clue.text: "It's good-night from me …", settling up in The Inn, Orpington

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the hidden letters are read from the bottom upwards
in says the letters are found inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: Someone says good night and pays their bill at a pub in Orpington.
explanation.walkthrough: Ronnie Corbett and Ronnie Barker closed The Two Ronnies with the lines 'It's good night from me' and 'And it's good night from him'. Orpington is a town in south-east London.
explanation.definitionFit: The line was one of the two Ronnies' sign-off on their BBC comedy show, so the catchphrase points to that first name.

clue.text: Refuse some luggage found in French station

indicators.note: found in says the piece of luggage sits inside the French station

parts.note: gare is the French word for a railway station
a bag is one piece of luggage

explanation.surface: A lost bag turns up at a railway station in France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Refuse' reads as a verb but is the noun, meaning rubbish.
explanation.definitionFit: As a noun, refuse is waste or rubbish, which is what garbage means.

clue.text: See 20
Those embarking on routine eleven irritating minutes late getting up to end of line (covered with more leaves)

indicators.note: to says the reversed initials are attached to the letter that comes before them
the end of a word is its final letter
in a down clue, getting up means those initials are read from the bottom upwards
the letters that embark on each word are the words' first letters

explanation.surface: A commuter grumbles that the usual eleven o'clock train is irritatingly late reaching the end of the line.
explanation.walkthrough: The initials R, E, I, M, L are read upwards to give LMIER, and the E from the end of 'line' goes on top.
explanation.definitionFit: Elmy describes a place thick with elm trees, and the comparative means more covered in elm foliage.

clue.text: Pointless infection from Cupid's Dart?

definitions.meaning: in tennis a score of zero, no points at all
Cupid's arrow makes its victim fall for someone

explanation.surface: A wry question about whether Cupid's arrow can pass on a meaningless disease.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means nil in tennis scoring, and is also the passion the god of desire's arrow brings on.

clue.text: See 11
Decline to retire a little ill-affected

indicators.note: to retire is to go back, so the hidden letters are read backwards
a little means only part of the following word supplies letters

explanation.surface: Someone who feels unwell declines to go to bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Decline to retire' reads as one phrase, but 'Decline' alone is the definition. The answer is also the first half of the theme's sitcom title.
explanation.definitionFit: A decline, a drop in level or value, is also called a fall.

clue.text: Shine a Light, following sweep

parts.note: F is the abbreviation for following, as in page references
to lash is to sweep or swing violently, as a tail does

explanation.surface: The Rolling Stones film Shine a Light is mentioned as coming after a sweeping movement.
explanation.definitionFit: To flash is to beam a lamp or torch briefly at something, which is shining a light on it.

clue.text: Domino's topping ratings, introducing comeback of Thunderball theme

indicators.note: the topping of a word is its first letter
introducing means one piece is brought inside the other

parts.note: ABs, able seamen, are naval ratings

indicators.note: a comeback runs the other way, so the film's number title is read backwards

parts.note: Thunderball was the fourth James Bond film, Bond IV

explanation.surface: Domino, the Bond girl in Thunderball, tops a ratings chart as the film's theme returns.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is just 'theme': this writer is the subject of the whole puzzle. Thunderball was the fourth Bond film, hence Bond IV.
explanation.definitionFit: The puzzle is a tribute to the comic novelist who created Reginald Perrin, so he is its subject.

clue.text: Party area? Too bad if nuts around

indicators.note: nuts means crazy, and the letters of the phrase are thrown about into a new order

explanation.surface: An area for a party, which would be a shame if crazy people were hanging about.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram of TOO BAD IF gives BIT OF A DO.
explanation.definitionFit: A do is informal British English for a celebration, and the phrase means something of an occasion.

clue.text: Rapid firing from above when reclining in office "fart-seats"

indicators.note: reclining says the hidden letters are read backwards
in says the letters lie inside the words that follow it

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Someone leans back on a whoopee cushion in the office.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft's definition took in 'when', but 'when' is a link word; the definition ends at 'above'. 'in' signals the hidden letters, which the draft left without an indicator.
explanation.definitionFit: To strafe is to attack from low-flying aircraft with machine-gun fire, which is rapid firing from above.

clue.text: See 24
Top journos' send-offs for one 10

indicators.note: a send-off is the end of something, so the last letters of the words are taken

explanation.surface: Leading journalists write farewell pieces for a well-known figure.
explanation.walkthrough: '10' stands for its answer's two words; their last letters, D and S, follow the E that ends 'one'. Send-offs here are also the obituaries editors would run on the writer's death.
explanation.definitionFit: Eds is short for editors, the senior journalists who run a paper.

clue.text: There can be no number determined to reverse direction

indicators.note: the compass direction south-east inside the phrase is turned around

parts.note: someone dead set on a thing is determined to do it

explanation.surface: A statement that no figure can be fixed in order to change course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'number' is not a figure but more numb. SE (south-east) in DEAD SET becomes ES.
explanation.definitionFit: Nothing can be more numb, that is number, than whatever is most lifeless.

clue.text: They could be fair pushing up the turf, as the old fellow's doing

indicators.note: in a down clue, pushing up means the word is read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: a sod is a piece of turf

explanation.surface: Flowers could be pushing up through the grass, as a dead old man is said to be doing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pushing up the turf' recalls pushing up the daisies, being dead and buried, which is what the old fellow is doing.
explanation.definitionFit: A fair is one kind of festive occasion, and such events are informally called dos.

clue.text: Good weather to avoid without heading initially for a 9ac…

indicators.note: in a down clue, a fall takes that letter lower, into the later word

parts.note: to shun is to avoid
sine is the Latin for without, as in sine die

indicators.note: initially picks out the opening letter of the word before it

explanation.surface: A forecaster's line on fine weather to dodge, heading for a downturn.
explanation.walkthrough: The H that starts 'heading' drops out of SHUN, leaving SUN, and falls into SINE to make SHINE. This clue runs on into 19-down, which completes the theme's firm.
explanation.definitionFit: Bright sun in a clear sky is the kind of weather people call good.

clue.text: Skirting artillery, snipe perhaps appears above ground

indicators.note: skirting means going round the edge, so the birds wrap round the gunners

parts.note: the snipe is one example of a bird
RA is the Royal Artillery

explanation.surface: A wading bird dodges gunfire and pops up out of the ground.
explanation.walkthrough: To braird is a Scots word for crops sprouting: the first shoots coming through the soil.
explanation.definitionFit: In Scots, a crop that brairds is putting its first green shoots up through the earth.

clue.text: See 24
… to be fair, they're just under great pressure to get a 27

indicators.note: in a down clue, getting a rise means the word is read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: someone stressed is under great pressure

explanation.surface: Continuing 16: fairly speaking, these people are heavily stressed while working for a pay rise.
explanation.walkthrough: Just deserts are what one fairly earns, and the phrase is often spelt with a double S. With 16 the answer gives the theme's firm, Sunshine Desserts, where Reggie Perrin works.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase 'just deserts', often spelt with a double S, means a fair reward or punishment, so these are what is just.

clue.text: Actor reprising De Niro's star role?

indicators.note: to reprise a role is to play it again in a fresh version, so these letters are reworked

explanation.surface: Robert De Niro returns to his most famous part.
explanation.walkthrough: This actor starred as Reggie Perrin in the BBC sitcom.
explanation.definitionFit: Rossiter was an English stage and screen performer, best known for Rising Damp and Reggie Perrin.

clue.text: See 29
French physicist's patron initially bein' human?

indicators.note: initially picks out the opening letter of the word before it

parts.note: 'to err is human', so erring is being human, clipped like bein'

explanation.surface: A question about whether a French scientist's backer is only human.
explanation.walkthrough: Jean Perrin won the 1926 Nobel Prize in Physics. The dropped G in 'bein'' signals the dropped G in ERRIN'.
explanation.definitionFit: Jean Perrin was a Nobel-winning French scientist who confirmed the existence of atoms, sharing the theme's surname.

clue.text: Pratt finally seen immersed in pure and simple poetry

indicators.note: immersed in means the letter is plunged inside the other word

parts.note: mere means nothing more than, pure and simple

indicators.note: finally picks out the last letter of the word before it

explanation.surface: Someone called Pratt is caught up in plain, unadorned verse.
explanation.definitionFit: Metre is the rhythmic pattern of verse, used here to stand for poetry as opposed to prose.

clue.text: Extremely Secret Army avoiding ransom? It's irregular

indicators.note: irregular means out of order, so the remaining letters are rearranged
avoiding means those letters are left out of the word

parts.note: RA is the Royal Artillery, the army's gunners

explanation.surface: A covert army refuses to pay a ransom, and is called irregular.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Secret Army' looks like one unit, but 'Extremely Secret' is the definition. NSOM (RANSOM less RA) plus IT is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Inmost means deepest or most private, so innermost thoughts are the most hidden ones.

clue.text: Tired Now, I'm Dead at Eighty — alternative title?

indicators.note: an alternative is a different version, so the letters are rearranged into another arrangement

parts.words: Tired Now, I'm Dead at Eighty

explanation.surface: A suggested memoir title for someone worn out and dying at eighty.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase was boss CJ's catchphrase in Reggie Perrin and the title of David Nobbs's memoir. Nobbs died in 2015 at eighty, hence the alternative.
explanation.definitionFit: The writer used his sitcom's catchphrase as the name of his autobiography, so it is a book title.

clue.text: Principally 4, rubbish or tat

indicators.note: principally means chiefly, so the leading letter of each word is taken

explanation.surface: A list of words for junk: garbage, rubbish or tat.
explanation.walkthrough: '4' is the answer to 4-down. Grot is also the shop in the sitcom where Reggie sells useless goods.
explanation.definitionFit: Grot is British slang for worthless junk, the same thing as garbage, rubbish and tat.

clue.text: Gimme that I don't unfortunately have right to accept

indicators.note: to accept means to take in, so the jumbled letters go inside

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: unfortunately means things have gone wrong, so these letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: Someone apologises that they have no right to take something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gimme that' is the whole definition: a curt demand, matched by the four-word phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are blunt demands for someone to pass an object over to the speaker.

clue.text: Difficult times: getting out of Civil Service, come back to life

indicators.note: getting out of means those letters leave the word

parts.note: crises are times of great difficulty

explanation.surface: A civil servant, through a hard spell, quits the job and feels revived.
explanation.walkthrough: The C and S come off either end of CRISES. With 9-across, the answer completes the sitcom's title.
explanation.definitionFit: To rise from the dead is to be resurrected and live again.

clue.text: Asian river followed a course westward? Yes and no

indicators.note: an across entry reads west to east, so westward means read backwards

parts.note: to run is to follow a course, as a river does
Y is the short form for yes, as on a Y/N form
N is the short form for no, as on a Y/N form

explanation.surface: Did an Asian river flow westwards? The answer is equivocal.
explanation.walkthrough: The Naryn flows through Kyrgyzstan and is a headwater of the Syr Darya.
explanation.definitionFit: The Naryn is a river in Central Asia, in Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan.

clue.text: For refreshing main taste, sup ___ _______

indicators.note: refreshing means giving something a new form, so these letters are reshuffled

explanation.surface: A recommendation to drink a named sparkling wine to freshen the palate.
explanation.walkthrough: The blanks are the answer's two words, so the whole clue reads as a toast.
explanation.definitionFit: Asti Spumante is a sweet sparkling Italian wine, the kind of drink one would sup to refresh the palate.
